body: The weekend flush has removed much of the leveraged long exposure that built up before the drop. That lowers the risk of another forced-selling cascade in the near term, but it does not bring in new buyers by itself. Sentiment is fragile. Several possible drivers are in play at once: ETF redemptions, rate-hike expectations and lingering exchange-security worries after the Binance hack. With that many headwinds, a recovery will need confirmation from flows rather than from price alone. Ether’s steeper loss keeps the ETH/BTC cross under pressure heading into the new week. Leveraged bulls paid for the weekend’s slide to a four-month low, and the bounce means little until ETF outflows stop. Bitcoin dropped to its lowest level since July over the weekend, trading as low as $62,000 before recovering to $64,910 by late Sunday afternoon US time, according to The Block’s price data. That still left the world’s largest cryptocurrency down 14.2% over the past seven days, and the selloff spread across the market to trigger roughly $2 billion in forced position closures. The damage was heavier further along the risk curve. Ether fell 18.2% over the week to $1,815, while Solana lost 19.7% to trade at $71.68, The Block reported. Ether underperforming bitcoin in a broad selloff is a familiar pattern, but a weaker ETH/BTC relationship on its own does not mean ether is cheap or due to catch up. CoinGlass hourly data showed crypto liquidations totalled $2.02 billion between 8 a.m. ET Saturday and 8 a.m. ET Sunday. Long positions accounted for $1.68 billion of that, against $342.4 million in shorts. A liquidation happens when an exchange closes a leveraged trade because the trader’s margin can no longer cover losses, and those forced sales can push prices lower and trigger the next round of liquidations. The roughly five-to-one skew toward longs shows that traders were leaning bullish with borrowed money going into the drop. By about 4:30 p.m. ET Sunday, the live 24-hour tally on CoinGlass had eased to $742.9 million as prices steadied. Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao used a post on X to deny rumours that the exchange had been selling crypto in the wake of its record hack on Oct. 29. Zhao said he had personally bought crypto over the past few days using stablecoins he recently received. He pointed to withdrawals from US spot bitcoin ETFs and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike as possible drivers of the slide, and suggested some investors may be raising cash for Anthropic’s planned IPO. He also cited lingering security concerns after the Binance hack. Those explanations are Zhao’s view rather than established causes. The ETF data does support part of that argument. US spot bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven straight trading sessions through Friday, The Block reported earlier. Spot ether ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, their seventh consecutive week of withdrawals and one short of the record run of eight. Outflows show reduced demand through these products, but they do not by themselves tell us who is selling or why. What to watch next: the first test is whether bitcoin can hold above the weekend low near $62,000 now that much of the leveraged long exposure has been cleared out. A halt to the ETF outflow streak, ideally confirmed over several completed sessions, would add evidence that product demand is stabilising. If spot ether ETFs post an eighth straight week of withdrawals, they would match their record. One calmer session after a liquidation flush is not proof of a bottom, so a practical approach is to watch both the flow trend and the price response before treating the recovery as durable. body: A flat quarter made weak mainly by trade is unlikely to derail BoJ tightening plans by itself. Strong capex and positive domestic demand are the parts policymakers watch most closely. The miss still gives the yen little help just as USD/JPY presses toward 160, and that raises the stakes for any comments from Japanese officials on the currency. JGB yields may ease slightly at the front end if traders trim December hike bets. The bigger driver for the session is Takata’s speech later today, where a hawkish response to the data would quickly restore conviction. For the Nikkei, softer growth and a weak yen are a familiar, broadly supportive mix for exporters. Japan’s Q3 stall was a trade story more than a domestic one: exports and cautious shoppers dragged, but strong business investment leaves the BoJ’s December hike case largely intact. Japan’s economy stalled in the July to September quarter. Preliminary data showed real GDP contracted at an annualised 0.1%, short of the 0.3% growth economists had expected and a sharp slowdown from 1.4% in the second quarter. On a quarterly basis, output was flat, against a forecast of a 0.1% gain. The miss came from two places. External demand subtracted 0.6 percentage point from growth, more than the 0.4 point drag expected, with exports slipping 0.2% from the previous quarter. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of the economy, fell 0.3%, a slightly deeper drop than the 0.2% decline forecast. Business investment was the bright spot. Capital expenditure jumped 1.6% from the prior quarter, just ahead of expectations of 1.5%, and reversed a 0.9% fall in the April to June period. Overall, domestic demand added 0.6 percentage point to growth, which shows the weakness was concentrated in trade rather than in the domestic economy as a whole. Price pressure across the economy also came in a little softer. The GDP deflator, a broad measure of prices across the economy, rose 2.4% from a year earlier, below forecasts and the previous quarter’s 2.6%, though still comfortably above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target. The figures land at a sensitive moment for the BoJ, which held its policy rate at 1.25% in October and is widely expected to raise it to 1.5% in December. A flat quarter driven by trade, alongside firm capital spending and positive domestic demand, gives policymakers grounds to look through the headline number. The softer consumption reading, however, will give more cautious board members something to point to. Attention now turns to BoJ board member Hajime Takata, who speaks later on Monday at 04:00 GMT (11:00 pm ET Sunday). Takata has dissented at recent meetings in favour of faster tightening, and his read on the data will be watched for any shift in the December debate. President Donald Trump has not made a public appearance since Wednesday, a gap that has stirred online speculation about his whereabouts. However, the official record of his activity over that period points to a president working out of view rather than one who is absent. The most recent sighting came on Thursday, when Trump recorded a video interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith inside the White House. On Saturday the White House called a travel and photo lid, the routine notice that the president will not be seen publicly that day. On Sunday, his published schedule showed him working from early morning until late evening on calls and meetings, and Trump posted on Truth Social that he was at the White House holding meetings on a range of subjects. Calendar entries also record a Sunday visit to his golf club and his return. The low profile has drawn attention largely because it overlapped with Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop, which Trump has not addressed in public. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has linked that disruption to faulty work on a telecom systems upgrade at a remote site, and the response so far has been led by cabinet officials. Some social media accounts have gone further, suggesting without evidence that the president is unwell or worse. Nothing in the public record supports that. Scrutiny of the schedule has run well ahead of the evidence, and the documented calendar, posts and official accounts describe his movements rather than any change in his health. Short absences like this are not new. Trump went about a week without a public appearance in late May and early June before returning to announce an executive order from the Oval Office. In April, during a similar quiet spell in the Iran war, the White House said he was working nonstop. The next clear test is his travel this week. Trump is expected to go to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, which would put him back in front of cameras within days. body: A services reading at a multi-year high, led by new orders, strengthens the case that New Zealand’s recovery is spreading beyond a handful of sectors. That gives the New Zealand dollar modest support on the domestic data front. For rate expectations, firmer activity reduces the pressure for further policy support. The flat employment reading and persistent cost-of-living complaints, however, point to slack that has not yet closed. Traders are likely to treat the data as a confidence builder rather than a game changer, and will look to the next few releases to see whether spending held back during the election starts to come through. New Zealand’s services firms are finally seeing new business arrive in volume heading into summer, but with hiring still flat, October’s strength looks more like a pre-Christmas lift than a recovery that has fully taken hold. New Zealand’s services sector expanded for a fifth consecutive month in October, with the BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index climbing to 51.7 from 50.9 in September. That is the strongest reading in more than three and a half years. A reading above 50 signals expansion. The gain was led by forward-looking measures. New orders and business rose to 53.0, activity and sales reached 52.6, and supplier deliveries came in at 52.1. Employment was the only sub-index in contraction, edging just below breakeven at 49.9, and stocks and inventories eased to 50.1. BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich said the run of readings above breakeven stood out against the past few years. She said it was encouraging to see activity and new business rising together heading into summer. She suggested that many firms had put decisions on hold before the election, and that some of that delayed spending and investment could start to come through by the end of the year once a new government is formed. Survey comments showed businesses are still preoccupied by fuel prices, the cost of living, interest rates and election uncertainty. On the positive side, respondents pointed to the run-in to summer, Christmas bookings and the return of tourists. The share of negative comments fell to 57.9% from 59.9% in September, a modest improvement in tone. Economists said firmer services activity is especially welcome because of the sector’s weight in the New Zealand economy and its importance for the GDP outlook. If the improvement holds, they said, it would add to evidence that the recovery is broadening and becoming more established. The softness in hiring is the main caveat. Firms appear willing to take on new business but are not yet adding staff. The next few months will show whether the election delay was the main drag on investment and jobs, or whether the caution runs deeper. Your market education doesn't end here. body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… The Middle East crisis and the spiking oil and gas prices have shifted the Asian nations’ priorities to energy security and generating electricity with homegrown resources. Renewable energy capacity is soaring, not only in the top emerging markets China and India, but also across Southeast Asia, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis hiked LNG prices and dented gas demand. Another clean energy source, nuclear capacity, is also gaining momentum globally. Countries worldwide started thinking about adding or building nuclear reactors for the first time in the wake of the previous energy crisis in 2022-2023. Construction will take years, but rising nuclear capacity could combine with the renewables surge to change the long-term gas and coal demand patterns in Asia’s economies. The world currently has 408 gigawatts (GW) of total operating nuclear power capacity. Another 91 GW is under construction, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s Global Nuclear Power Tracker . Of the 91 GW of nuclear capacity in the construction stage, as much as 73%, or 66 GW, are in Asia, per the data compiled by Reuters columnist Gavin Maguire. Asia also leads in utility solar and wind power construction, as smaller emerging markets add to powerhouses China and India in boosting their renewable energy capacities. China and India still rely on coal for a large part of their electricity supply and continue to approve and build coal-fired power plants, but they are also betting big on nuclear and renewables to meet soaring electricity demand. Globally, China, India, Japan, and South Korea are the top four countries currently building the most nuclear power capacity in the world, according to the Global Energy Monitor (GEM) data. China leads with more than 43 GW under construction, followed by India with 6.6 GW, Japan with 6.1 GW, and South Korea with 5.6 GW. China, the world’s second-largest economy after the U.S., is not picking one electricity source over another—it is building more of everything to meet rising demand. China is a global leader in coal, renewables, and nuclear power additions and planned projects as its primary goal is energy security and fewer fossil fuel imports at low prices, preferably. India has also become a renewable energy powerhouse in recent years. India has also boosted battery and other energy storage to support the rapid expansion of solar PV capacity installations, but it needs much more to ensure the curtailment rates of renewable energy are reduced. The world’s most populous country, while still betting big on coal power capacity, has huge plans in the nuclear power sector, too. India’s goal is to boost its installed nuclear power capacity to 100 GW by 2047, up from just 8.8 GW now. At the end of 2025, India’s government approved the landmark Atomic Energy Bill, which allows private companies to invest in its nuclear energy industry for the first time, as the country looks to boost nuclear power capacity tenfold within two decades. Moreover, India expects to build five small modular reactors (SMRs) domestically by 2033, India’s Atomic Energy Minister, Jitendra Singh, said earlier this year. Japan has made a U-turn in nuclear energy policy and plans to rely more on nuclear reactors for its power supply in the coming decades. title: Oil prices steady as Middle East tensions persist - The Vibes
body: Brent holds near US$95.50 and WTI at US$88.50 a barrel as investors weigh renewed attacks in the Gulf against expectations of a global supply surplus CRUDE oil prices were largely unchanged on Monday as renewed hostilities in the Middle East kept supply concerns in focus, while expectations of an improving global supply balance limited further gains. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude traded around US$88.50 a barrel, while Brent crude hovered near US$95.50 after sharp price swings last week. Tensions escalated after Iran struck a US helicopter base in Bahrain on Sunday, marking its first attack on a Persian Gulf state in several weeks. Iranian state television also reported that five vessels had struck mines, while maritime authorities confirmed an attack on a tanker. All crew members were reported safe. However, hopes of a diplomatic resolution remained after Tehran indicated that negotiations were still possible, while US President Donald Trump said further strikes against Iran might not be necessary. Adding to the pressure on oil prices, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reported last week that global oil supply had exceeded demand for the first time since the conflict began. It projected a surplus of about two million barrels per day this quarter as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz gradually recover. On the currency front, the US Dollar Index (DXY), which measures the greenback against a basket of six major currencies, slipped 0.03 per cent to 103.379. The index has declined 1.37 per cent over the past four weeks but gained 3.81 per cent over the past 12 months. The US dollar also edged lower against the ringgit, with the USD/MYR exchange rate falling 0.04 per cent to 4.0845. body: The October consumer price index rose 0.4% from the month before, a tenth of a point above the 0.3% that economists had forecast. Food and shelter costs led the advance. Core CPI — which excludes food and energy — also registered 0.3%, matching its pace from each of the previous two months. The Bureau of Labor Statistics published the data on November 10. A monthly core reading around 0.2% would put annual inflation on course for the Fed's 2% target. Three consecutive months at 0.3% push the annualized three-month rate to 3.7%, the fastest clip of the year. The report carried an unusual footnote: federal statisticians were unable to publish an official 12-month CPI comparison because no price data were collected in October 2025, when a government shutdown halted the surveys. The Producer Price Index for October, released November 13, reinforced the picture. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% on the month and 6.5% on the year — the highest annual rate since November 2022, according to the BLS. Final-demand goods drove much of the increase, up 0.5%, while the services component edged 0.2% higher. Prices for truck transportation of freight surged 3.9%, accounting for more than 80% of the increase in final-demand services. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, in an interview on PBS NewsHour after the report, described the data as "borderline disturbing," warning that "we have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing." Until recently, the internal Fed debate focused on the timing of rate cuts. That calculus flipped after the October numbers landed. Fed Governor Christopher Waller, speaking at a Bank of England conference in London on the day the CPI was released, said he would support a 25-basis-point increase at the December meeting. He added that if core inflation came in around 0.3% or higher, a 50-basis-point move should be considered as well. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan was more direct: she said the FOMC needs at least two additional quarter-point hikes, followed by a pause to assess conditions. James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, told CBS News in an email that the October CPI report was the last look at inflation the Fed would get before its December meeting, adding that "it most likely seals the deal on a rate hike to close the year." Futures markets already reflect the shift. As of this writing, traders are fully pricing a quarter-point hike at the FOMC's December 8-9 meeting. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — climbed from 3.4% in August to 3.6% in September. The Cleveland Fed's real-time model projects the PCE rate will reach 3.77% in October and 3.82% in November, extending the gap above the 2% target. The timing presents a procedural challenge. The November CPI report won't be published until December 10 — one day after the FOMC votes. Policymakers will have to decide without seeing the latest consumer-price reading. The reversal from expected cuts to probable hikes carries direct consequences. Mortgage rates, as measured by the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Survey , already stand near 7.18%. Consumer credit, auto loans, and business financing remain expensive or could become more so. For families that have already stretched budgets against years of elevated living costs , an additional tightening cycle is not a financial abstraction — it is tangible monthly pressure. Inflation has now run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. The data are on the table. The Federal Reserve's December meeting is three weeks away.

body: Most economists expect the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) to keep interest rates unchanged when the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meets later this week, although a further 25-basis-point increase remains possible. Neil Roets, CEO of Debt Rescue, said the SARB faces a difficult decision, with inflation remaining above its target while consumers continue to struggle under the combined pressure of high living and borrowing costs. “Our expectation is that the Monetary Policy Committee will lean towards keeping interest rates unchanged, although a further 25-basis-point increase remains a possibility,” Roets said. He said inflation had increased to 4.5% in September from 4.4% in August, showing that price pressures remained a concern. However, recent declines in international oil prices offered some encouragement, although ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East meant that sustained improvement was far from guaranteed. Roets said these developments strengthened the case for allowing previous interest rate decisions more time to work through the economy before further tightening was considered. The release of October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) figures on 19 November, shortly before the MPC announcement, would also be important, he said. The data could provide further insight into whether previous monetary policy measures were beginning to produce the desired results. Roets added that many South African households had already absorbed years of rising living costs. Even when inflation slows, accumulated increases in essential expenses remain part of monthly budgets. “Declining international oil prices do not automatically translate into immediate reductions in fuel, transport or food costs,” he said. “A further interest rate increase would place additional pressure on households with variable-rate debt, particularly home loans and vehicle finance.” Johann Els, chief economist at PSG Financial Services, said that, on balance, the Reserve Bank was likely to leave interest rates unchanged. “Policy has done enough,” Els said. “There hasn’t been any serious second-round effect in inflation. The Reserve Bank has indicated that policy is restrictive, although there are still risks in terms of second-round effects.” Benay Sager, executive head of DebtBusters, also expects the interest rate to remain unchanged for now. “We do foresee a change in January, but it’s too difficult to say at the moment whether that will be an increase or decrease,” Sager said. title: AI Data Center Stocks Crater On Nebius Outlook And Nvidia Uncertainty, But Applied Digital's (NASDAQ: APLD) $36.2B Lease Book Remains Intact - Foreign Policy Journal
body: A $36.2 billion portfolio of signed, non-cancellable leases did nothing to shield Applied Digital (NASDAQ: APLD) from a brutal morning session, as shares slid 10% despite zero company-specific news. The selloff swept across the AI infrastructure sector, with Nebius (NASDAQ: NBIS) dropping 13%, CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) losing roughly 10%, IREN (NASDAQ: IREN) shedding 10%, and Cipher Digital (NASDAQ: CIFR) falling 9%. The catalyst was Nebius, whose third-quarter revenue surged 571% to $980.8 million but included $325.1 million in non-recurring strategic partnership payments that raised quality-of-earnings questions. Bank of America flagged that Nebius’s guidance implies a sequential revenue decline in the fourth quarter, with delays at third-party data centers pushing recognized revenue into early 2027. A separate and arguably more alarming disclosure was a $40 billion capital spending plan for 2027, which rattled investors already sensitive to the pace of AI infrastructure buildout. Nvidia’s leadership transition compounded the anxiety, as The Information reported that the chipmaker is expected to pull back on AI investments and credit guarantees following Jensen Huang’s exit as CEO on Thursday. That report hit IREN particularly hard, given that Nvidia represents a $3.4 billion customer relationship for the company, while Cipher fell alongside news from the Wall Street Journal that private neocloud Nscale requires additional financing before its planned IPO. None of these developments altered a single dollar of Applied Digital’s contracted revenue, where two anchor tenants account for 86% of the total signed lease value: a tier-one hyperscaler holding $20.2 billion and CoreWeave holding $11 billion across 15-year agreements. CoreWeave’s own financial position draws scrutiny, with its bonds yielding above 17%, yet the leases carry no cancellation provisions and CoreWeave pays approximately 10% more per megawatt than hyperscaler peers. Wall Street expects Applied Digital’s revenue to more than triple between fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2028, with minimum lease payments alone projected to reach $1.58 billion in fiscal 2028, representing around 80% of that year’s consensus estimate. At today’s depressed price, Applied Digital trades at well under 5x forward sales, compared to a three-year average multiple of roughly 11x, a gap that suggests the market is pricing in risks beyond what the contracted backlog justifies. The genuine vulnerability is not the tenants but the capital required to bring additional capacity online: CEO Wes Cummins stated this month that the company must still finance approximately 800 MW over the coming 12 months. A sustained sector selloff raises the cost and complexity of that financing, meaning the fiscal second-quarter earnings report due in January becomes the sector’s next real stress test.

China’s economy is running on one engine: AI exports are holding up growth while factories slow, shoppers retreat and property keeps sliding, and Beijing seems content to wait until that engine falters. China’s factory output slowed more than expected in October and consumer spending stayed weak, raising fresh questions about how long the world’s second-largest economy can lean on exports to carry growth, Reuters reported. Industrial output rose 4.8% from a year earlier, official data showed on Monday, short of the 5.3% forecast and down from 5.5% in September. An official survey had already pointed to softer manufacturing sentiment in October, with new orders and new export orders weakening. That was despite trade data last week showing goods exports surging on demand for AI-related technology. Retail sales grew just 0.4%, down from 1.1% in September and below the 0.8% expected. That is a weak result for a month that included a seven-day national holiday and the start of the Singles Day shopping festival. Growth in services spending also eased slightly, to 4.9% in the first ten months. A statistics bureau spokesperson acknowledged that households’ ability and willingness to spend need to improve. The property slump remains the biggest drag. New home prices fell again in October, extending their run of monthly declines to 41 months, while resale prices posted a 42nd straight fall. The annual decline in new home prices did ease to 2.4% from 2.8%, the slowest since November 2025. Shanghai was the only major city to record rises in both new and resale prices. Property investment fell 21.6% in the first ten months, with new construction starts down 24.4%. Housing is the main store of household wealth, so falling values push families to save rather than spend. Economists say prices need to stabilise across cities, and excess inventory needs to clear, before the sector can recover. Broader investment deteriorated further. Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first ten months, worse than the 7.0% decline expected and the steepest drop in this year’s run of contractions. The one positive was unemployment, which edged down to 5.1% from 5.2%. Even so, economists do not expect a rush of new policy. With third-quarter growth at 4.5%, Beijing still looks on track for its annual target, and some analysts said they expect no new stimulus for the rest of the year. Others described 2026 as one of the weakest years for domestic demand in recent history. They said support for consumption could build in 2027, especially if exports start to cool and the drag from earlier trade-in subsidies fades. Japan’s shoppers are buckling under inflation, but rather than giving the BOJ a reason to pause, the squeeze on households is being read as further proof that rates need to keep rising. Japan’s economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter as rising living costs forced households to cut back on spending. Economists say the weakness is unlikely to knock the Bank of Japan off its tightening path, Reuters reported. Gross domestic product fell an annualised 0.1%, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth, following an upwardly revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. It was the first contraction in four quarters. On a quarterly basis, output slipped 0.02%, versus expectations of a 0.1% rise. Households did most of the damage. Private consumption, which makes up more than half of economic output, fell 0.3%, slightly worse than the expected 0.2% drop. Persistent inflation, heavy rain and typhoons weighed on spending. Purchases of cars and air conditioners also fell back after a temporary boost from tax and regulatory changes in the prior quarter. Economists warned that higher prices linked to Middle East tensions will keep squeezing households’ purchasing power, even as wages rise. Trade also took away from growth. Net external demand cut 0.6 percentage point, more than the expected 0.4 point drag. Imports jumped as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified its supply following disruption from the war in the Middle East. Business investment was the bright spot. It rose 1.6% against a 1.5% forecast, supported by spending on labour-saving technology and AI-related projects. Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said better employment and income conditions, along with policy measures, should support a gradual recovery, but stressed the need to monitor the Middle East situation closely. Several argued that weak consumption is itself a symptom of high prices, which strengthens the case for further hikes, and many expect the next move as soon as December. The widely anticipated move marked the bank's first hike since Aug. 2023, and made it the last major central bank to embark on a tightening cycle since the U.S. and Israel went to war with Iran eight months ago. The majority of the bank's Monetary Policy Committee voted for the quarter-point hike, with the motion passing by 8 votes to 1. The dissenting member voted to raise the bank's key interest rate by 50 basis points to 4.25%. "The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month," the MPC said in a statement Thursday. "Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level." Policymakers said they now expected U.K. inflation to rise to "about 5%" by the middle of 2027. "It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation," they said. Ahead of the decision being announced, markets had been pricing in more than a 99% chance of a rate hike, according to LSEG data. Traders were also pricing in a one-in-four chance of a further hike in December. Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in the November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside." "Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics," he said. Data released earlier this month showed that the U.K.'s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.5% in September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. As a net energy importer, the U.K. is particularly vulnerable to external energy shocks — such as the one caused this year by the Iran war. The MPC's most hawkish member, Catherine L Mann, said she had voted for greater tightening than her peers because research pointed to "non-linear inflation risks." "My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a 'down payment' to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold 'good policy'," she said in comments published in the MPC's policy statement. "The economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects," Mann added. "A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off... From a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is 'good policy'." Goldman’s second downgrade and warnings of ETF selling point to the same problem for gold: a Fed that keeps hiking leaves little room for a quick recovery, even with central banks still buying. Goldman Sachs has lowered its end-2027 gold price forecast to $4,650 an ounce from $4,800, its second downgrade in a month, as expectations of a longer run of Federal Reserve rate hikes cloud the outlook for investor demand, Investing.com reported. The bank’s economists now expect the Fed to deliver a third quarter-point increase in March 2027, on top of the December hike that was already in Goldman’s base case. A rising policy rate is likely to weigh on private-sector investment in gold through early next year, even as central banks keep buying. In practice, the new target lines up with the bear-case scenario Goldman flagged in its previous note, which effectively moves that outcome into the main forecast. Goldman’s first cut, earlier this month, lowered its end-2026 target to $4,150 from $4,650 and its end-2027 target to $4,800 from $5,400. The bank remains constructive over the longer run. It expects central banks to buy around 60 tonnes a month through 2026 and 2027. title: Goldman Sachs Sees 2 Million Barrel-a-Day Oil Glut in 2027; Brent to Hit $78 by Year-End - BigGo Finance
body: Global investment bank Goldman Sachs forecasts that the international crude oil market will enter a clear supply glut in 2027, putting downward pressure on prices. Even with supply disruption risks still lingering, production is expected to far outstrip consumption demand, according to the analysis. Goldman Sachs analysts including Daan Struyven estimated in a Nov. 15 report that, under the base case, excess supply—production minus final consumption demand—will reach 2 million barrels per day in 2027. That figure already reflects the possibility of supply disruptions amounting to 1 million barrels per day. They projected that Brent crude futures will average $88 a barrel (~100,000 won) next year before falling to $78 a barrel (~90,000 won) by year-end. The decline is expected to widen as the risk premium gradually normalizes. This year, the global oil market experienced significant volatility due to the US-Iran War. In the early stages of the conflict, crude production in the Middle East contracted, but supply later recovered as producers used alternative export routes and resumed shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The International Energy Agency (IEA) said last week that the global oil market is set to shift into oversupply for the first time since the war broke out. "2027 will see a continued tug-of-war between high supply disruption risks and the market's expanding capacity to adapt," the Goldman Sachs analysts said. "In the base case, Middle East supply will exceed its 2025 average through ship-to-ship crude transfers and pipeline expansions, while supply growth outside the Middle East will stagnate." China, the world's largest crude importer, is also unlikely to prop up oil prices. The analysts said weak road-transport fuel consumption in China will drag down crude demand by about 400,000 barrels per day, adding that "China's total oil demand is estimated to have peaked in 2025." Brent crude surged above $126 a barrel (~170,000 won) intraday in April this year, the highest since 2022, and has averaged about $91 a barrel (~120,000 won) so far this year. It recently traded below $95 a barrel (~130,000 won), down about 1%. The forecast comes as the crude supply chain undergoes restructuring. While export route diversification and pipeline expansions by Middle East producers are driving a supply recovery, structural slowdown in China is becoming pronounced on the demand side, tilting the supply-demand balance in favor of supply, according to the assessment. The market is treating the report as a key indicator for the direction of energy prices from next year onward. If the supply glut materializes, pressure on producers to cut output could intensify, and it could ease cost burdens for Asia's refining and chemicals sectors, which rely heavily on crude imports, according to some observations. On the other hand, some analysts suggest it could pose downward pressure on earnings forecasts for energy companies. Learn more. ) Among the crude oil varieties traded internationally, WTI, short for West Texas Intermediate, ranks as one of the three major types alongside Brent and Dubai Crude. Its relatively low gravity and sulphur content account for the descriptions “light” and “sweet”, respectively. Regarded as a high-quality oil, it is easy to refine. Produced in the United States, WTI is distributed through the Cushing hub, known as “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. WTI serves as an oil-market benchmark, and its price is regularly cited in media reports. Supply and demand underpin WTI Oil prices, as they do prices of other assets. Stronger global growth can lift demand, whereas weaker growth can have the reverse effect. On the supply side, political instability, wars and sanctions can cause disruptions that affect prices. Decisions by OPEC, the group of major oil-producing countries, are another important influence. Since oil trades predominantly in US Dollars, movements in the currency also matter for WTI Crude Oil prices: a weaker US Dollar can make oil more affordable, while a stronger dollar can have the opposite effect. WTI Oil prices respond to the weekly oil inventory releases from the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA), as stock movements indicate shifts in supply and demand. Falling inventories can signal stronger demand and lift oil prices; rising inventories can suggest greater supply and weigh on prices. The API releases its report on Tuesdays, followed by the EIA the next day. The two reports generally produce similar results, with the figures within 1% of one another 75% of the time. As the EIA is a government agency, its data is regarded as more reliable. Production quotas agreed by OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) often influence WTI Oil prices.

In the near term, though, the market is still driven by the war. Confirmation of the IRGC’s tanker-sinking claims could quickly rebuild the risk premium that Goldman expects to fade. Monday’s dip suggests traders are leaning toward the surplus story for now. The diesel forecast matters for inflation. At $150 a barrel, products stay costly even as crude eases, so energy keeps feeding into the inflation concerns Fed officials raised over the weekend. Goldman’s message on oil is patience: a surplus is coming and prices should fall, but until the Gulf calms down, the risks over the next few weeks still point upward. Goldman Sachs expects oil prices to drift lower over the next year as the market returns to surplus. It forecasts Brent crude to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and ease to $78 by December 2027, though it warned of upside risks in the near term from attacks on shipping in the Middle East, Reuters reported. For US crude, the bank sees West Texas Intermediate averaging $78 a barrel next year and slipping to $70 by the end of 2027. Refined products should also ease but stay well above historical norms, with US wholesale diesel forecast to average $150 a barrel in 2027. The core of the call is supply. In Goldman’s base case, oil production will exceed end-use demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027. That surplus is large enough to pull prices down from current levels, even if some war-related risk premium lingers. The bank was careful to present the risks as running in both directions. In the near term, it said prices could rise if attacks on shipping intensify, if oil infrastructure is damaged or if the risk premium rebuilds. Over the medium term, the risk is to the downside, through stronger supply, weaker demand or a smaller risk premium than it assumes. That near-term risk is real. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed over the weekend that two tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and that one of them, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels, sank. There has been no independent confirmation. Even so, prices fell on Monday on expectations of a supply surplus. Shipments through Hormuz were reported to be close to pre-war levels, and Washington eased domestic fuel movements by extending its Jones Act waiver. Brent was trading around $95.50 earlier in Asia, well above Goldman’s 2027 average, which implies significant downside if the bank’s surplus view plays out. The gap between today’s prices and the forecast path leaves the oil market hinging on one question: whether supply disruption in the Gulf fades or flares up again. summary: Bitcoin's ongoing weakness has pushed it below key technical support levels, triggering the cascade of long liquidations into the weekend.
body: Bitcoin fell to its lowest levels since August over the weekend as a wave of forced liquidations accelerated amid broader weakening in market liquidity and risk appetite. The price of the flagship cryptocurrency fell as low as $62,000 late Saturday, according to Coin Metrics, and is coming off its sixth weekly decline in a row. On Monday morning, it had climbed back to the $64,000 level. Bitcoin's ongoing weakness pushed its price below key technical support levels during the week, breaking below its 200-day moving average of about $73,000 and triggering the cascade of long liquidations, forcing traders to sell their assets at market price to settle their debts, pushing prices lower. On Saturday night, exchanges tracked by CoinGlass saw more than $165 million in liquidated bitcoin long positions, following $629 million on Friday and nearly $700 million on Thursday. Bitcoin was also facing potential selling pressure ahead of Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering, with the listing drawing speculative capital away from riskier assets. On Friday, the dollar index — which has an inverse relationship with bitcoin — reached its highest level since April 2025, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening. That pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pressuring both bitcoin and gold, despite their appeal as alternative stores of value in the longer term. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from the combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. "A break below $60,000 is possible if Nvidia's results add to the tech selling," he said. "The catalysts for a move higher are mostly macro, and a softer dollar with falling real yields would ease the pressure on every risk asset at once. If that happens, bitcoin goes into the recovery with less leverage than it carried in October, and a close back above $73,000 would be the first sign that the selling is over." Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization platform Brickken, said he's monitoring whether spot buyers step in once the forced selling subsides. "Clearing out leveraged longs can slow the selling," he said. body: Days after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the chipmaker he founded 33 years ago, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress will now face intense questions about what comes next. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly earnings after the close on Tuesday. While the company is again expected to show explosive growth as the key infrastructure provider to the artificial intelligence boom, Kress and her team will likely be forced to answer questions on chip sales to China, the risks tied to deals with neoclouds and what comes next under new leadership. Huang resigned Thursday, but Nvidia's legions of customers, partners and investors still rely on the company to continue shipping large quantities of graphics processing units and AI systems. Kress, who has been Nvidia's CFO since 2013, was tapped to lead the company while the board searches for a successor. Analysts expect Nvidia to report 91% revenue growth to $109.1 billion, according to LSEG, with $2.47 in earnings per share. Kress, alongside Huang, offered a full-year growth forecast suggesting that the company's historic expansion is poised to continue. They said revenue expansion in fiscal 2028 would be roughly 70% in what Kress, on the last earnings call, described as a "supply constrained outlook." "What would be good for them to do is reiterate that and confirm that is still intact, if they have the ability," said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kunjan Sobhani. But Kress has to do far more than just put up numbers. The stock has dropped for six straight weeks, the longest losing streak since 2012, pushing the company's market cap down by $1.7 trillion. Huang's public downfall began in October, when The New York Times reported that American intelligence agencies were surveilling a woman named Alice Huang, who was close with the former CEO, believing she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The report alleged that Alice Huang was helping smuggle Nvidia's premium chips into China, violating U.S. export controls. An Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the report saying, "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Nvidia has also insisted that it gets essentially no data center sales from China, consistent with how it reports sales in its recent Securities and Exchange Commission filings. But Jensen Huang's romantic ties to Alice Huang, a Megaspeed International executive, raised concerns about Nvidia's actual business in China. Culper Research, a short selling research firm that published a note on Nvidia's "China problem" in May, alleges that 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was "driven by China." Nvidia has denied any diversion, and said it has no evidence that any such activity has taken place. But that was before last week's scandal. However, foreign policy remains largely within the president’s remit, as demonstrated by his interventions in Venezuela this year, from the capture of Nicolas Maduro to the reopening of the country’s oil sector. These developments have highlighted how closely Venezuela’s oil recovery is tied to decisions in Washington. However, Rystad Energy’s analysis suggests that Venezuela’s near-term oil recovery is unlikely to be derailed by the latest election result. The bigger risk lies further down the line, as increased congressional scrutiny could delay around 0.5 million bpd of potential production growth until after 2040. Venezuela’s near-term recovery is being driven primarily by brownfield activity, including well reactivations, workovers and infill drilling. These projects have shorter lead times and require fewer new approvals, supporting crude production growth from approximately 1.2 million bpd in October 2026 to around 1.5 million bpd by 2028, an increase of roughly 300,000 bpd. Sanctions implementation and licensing by the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also remain largely under executive control, limiting what a Democratic Congress can change directly. The picture becomes less certain further out, as growth increasingly depends on greenfield developments, larger investment commitments and the operators selected to deliver them. Rystad Energy’s existing upside scenario sees Venezuelan production approaching 3 million bpd by 2040, assuming stronger prices and continued policy support. A new sensitivity following the midterm result suggests greater congressional scrutiny could delay selected greenfield projects by one to three years, pushing around 0.5 million bpd of potential 2040 production further out. The impact is concentrated in longer-cycle projects rather than the brownfield-led recovery expected over the next few years. However, that growth will be harder to deliver if political scrutiny delays or challenges operators' ability to develop their assets. North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) is a case in point. Its three production participation contracts have lifted combined output from roughly 90,000 barrels per day (bpd) at the end of 2024 to nearly 200,000 bpd currently, led by Petrozamora. The company is already facing questions from Democratic lawmakers over its selection and the legal basis for its agreements, raising broader questions about Venezuela's operating environment and its ability to attract investment to sustain longer-term recovery. Greater scrutiny doesn’t change Venezuela’s underlying resource potential. Most of the near-term recovery involves bringing existing wells back online, which doesn’t require congressional approval, so I wouldn’t expect the midterms to slow that down. The bigger risk is to greenfield projects, which could be delayed by several years. The oil isn’t going anywhere, but it may take longer to reach the market. title: Canadian Natural’s $1.77 billion Advantage takeover fuels Alberta oil expansion
summary: The Canadian energy giant will acquire Advantage Energy's Montney assets as consolidation in the oilpatch accelerates.
body: Canadian Natural Resources (TSX, NYSE: CNQ) is acquiring Advantage Energy (TSX: AAV) in a C$2.53-billion ($1.77-billion) deal that will expand its oil and natural gas production in Alberta as consolidation accelerates across Canada’s energy sector. The all-cash transaction, announced Monday, values Advantage at C$13.55 per share, a premium of nearly 25% to Friday’s closing price. The offer represents an equity value of approximately C$2.26 billion, with the total transaction value including net debt and outstanding convertible debentures. “The transaction is the result of a comprehensive review of strategic alternatives,” Advantage said in a separate statement . The acquisition comes as Canadian producers seek to expand output and strengthen their positions in established oil and gas regions. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has also moved to encourage investment through proposed legislation aimed at reducing regulatory hurdles and accelerating approvals for major natural resource projects. The deal will add approximately 79,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of production from Advantage’s Montney and Charlie Lake assets, along with an inventory of light crude oil and liquids-rich natural gas development opportunities. The properties are adjacent to Canadian Natural’s existing operations in the Grande Prairie area of Alberta, offering opportunities to integrate production and infrastructure while expanding its regional resource base. Advantage’s assets also include significant natural gas processing capacity, notably the Glacier Gas Plant, which can handle 425 million cubic feet per day, and the newly commissioned Progress Gas Plant, with capacity of 75 million cubic feet per day. Canadian Natural will also assume responsibility for satisfying obligations tied to Advantage’s C$143.75 million in outstanding 5% convertible unsecured subordinated debentures due in 2029. The acquisition adds to a wave of multibillion-dollar transactions reshaping Canada’s oil and gas industry as larger producers pursue scale, operational efficiencies and access to established resource basins. Tamarack Valley Energy (TSX: TVE) and Headwater Exploration (TSX: HWX) have agreed to merge in a C$10-billion deal, while Cenovus Energy (TSX, NYSE: CVE) has announced plans to acquire Athabasca Oil (TSX: ATH) in a C$5.7-billion transaction. The transactions highlight an industry-wide push to consolidate production and development opportunities as companies position themselves for longer-term growth. Canadian Natural’s acquisition is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, adding another major transaction to a sector increasingly dominated by large, integrated producers. title: Banking giant sets silver price for 2027 - Finbold
body: Silver could average $70 per ounce in 2027, with prices reaching $75 during the second and third quarters, according to a forecast by Bank of America ( BofA ). In its outlook published on November 16, BofA analysts led by Michael Widmer projected a quarterly average of $75 in the second and third quarters, while maintaining a full-year average forecast of $70. As of press time, silver was trading at $47 per ounce, down 3.1% for the week and well below its January 26 record of $121. From that level, the metal would need to gain approximately 56.3% to reach BofA’s $75 target. One of the main factors supporting the forecast is the prospect of tightening supply conditions. BofA expects the silver market to move from an estimated 910-tonne surplus in 2026 to an 852-tonne deficit in 2027, following an estimated 8,600-tonne deficit in 2025. The projected surplus this year reflects weaker investor demand and declining solar-sector consumption, partly driven by efforts to reduce silver use through thrifting and technological improvements. However, a return to a deficit next year could tighten the physical market and support prices. Investor demand will also remain important. BofA notes that physically backed silver exchange-traded funds ( ETFs ) attracted approximately 8.6 kilotonnes of inflows in 2025 but have recorded outflows of around 1.5 kilotonnes so far in 2026. A reversal in these flows could strengthen silver’s recovery as investors return to precious metals. Growing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure could also boost silver consumption. To this end, BofA estimates that hyperscale data centres require approximately 708,000 ounces of silver per gigawatt of capacity, compared with around 318,000 ounces for traditional enterprise data centres. The bank expects global data-centre capacity to increase from approximately 130 gigawatts in 2026 to 240 gigawatts by 2030. Consequently, silver demand from data centres could more than double from approximately 270 tonnes this year to over 600 tonnes by 2030. However, the sector is expected to account for less than 2% of global silver consumption, leaving investment flows and established industrial applications as more significant price drivers. BofA’s forecast is more bullish than those of other major institutions. JPMorgan expects silver to average $63 per ounce in 2027, while the World Bank’s October outlook puts the figure at $62. Meanwhile, the Silver Institute expects the market to record its sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with a projected shortfall of 35 million ounces. However, total demand is forecast to decline 5% to 1.08 billion ounces, including a 3% drop in industrial consumption and a 22% decline in jewellery demand. Silver recycling is also expected to rise 6% to 210 million ounces, potentially offsetting some supply constraints.

body: WASHINGTON (AP) — Artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in an era of faster economic growth, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday in remarks that also acknowledged risks from the technology. The adoption of AI could also lead to widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market if the healthy returns expected from the huge investments in AI infrastructure don't materialize, Warsh said. But he did not mention inflation, even though many of his colleagues blame the buildout of data centers for accelerating price increases . Warsh's remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the Fed's San Francisco branch. The Fed chairman did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates, nor did he say anything about recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month . That data led many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee to signal their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. "What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation," Warsh said. "It appears to be changing the method — and, at least as important, the speed — of innovation. If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average." The Fed refers to AI as "super intelligence" following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Yet Warsh also spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI then he has in previous speeches. The Chairman has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation. In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rate under that scenario. "As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free," Warsh said. "And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly." For example, "after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added. The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. Warsh on Monday did not address AI's impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week . In addition, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. "If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms' desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates," Jefferson said.

If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average.” The Fed refers to AI as “super intelligence” following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Yet Warsh also spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI then he has in previous speeches. The Chairman has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation. In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rate under that scenario. “As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free,” Warsh said. “And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly.” For example, “after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment,” he said. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added. The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. Warsh on Monday did not address AI's impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week . In addition, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. “If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms’ desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates," Jefferson said. title: Nvidia turmoil tests Bitcoin miners' AI funding plans amid leadership changes - TradingView
body: Jensen Huang is out as Nvidia's CEO. The timing is awkward for Bitcoin miners, who have been betting billions that AI data centers can be their next act. The leadership shake-up lands just as a Texas permit freeze and a wave of analyst downgrades put the economics of the miner-to-AI pivot under a microscope. Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on November 12, 2026. CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first board chair. The market reaction was swift. Nvidia shares fell by as much as 12% intraday, contributing to an estimated $500 billion to $855 billion in market-cap losses over the course of the week. The selling didn't stay contained. Following the resignation, IREN stock dropped about 6.5% and MARA slid about 6%, alongside broader declines across AI-related names. Then there's Texas. The state halted new data-center permits in September 2026, a decision with outsized consequences because approximately 25-30% of planned US AI capacity is linked to the state. Newly elected governor Gina Hinojosa has committed to keeping that moratorium in place until lawmakers set rules on electricity and water costs. Analysts had already started recalibrating before Nvidia's news broke. In early November 2026, Bernstein cut price targets on AI-pivoted miners by 35-54%, pointing to financing concerns and regulatory uncertainty in Texas. Morgan Stanley was also among the firms trimming targets on AI-focused miners. Bitcoin miners spent years building the one thing AI companies now crave: large sites with access to massive amounts of power. Pivoting that infrastructure toward high-performance computing looked like an obvious upgrade. Several miners have already signed multibillion-dollar AI and HPC hosting agreements with major users of Nvidia GPUs, including CoreWeave. Some have also lined up partnerships involving companies like Microsoft and Nvidia itself. The combined pressure from Nvidia's leadership change and the Texas freeze is drawing a clear line through the sector. On one side sit miners whose AI projects are already funded or already permitted. On the other are those still hunting for money and approvals. Raising capital gets harder when analysts are cutting targets by as much as 54%, and a project that depends on a new Texas permit has no clear start date while the moratorium holds. For anyone holding AI-pivoted mining stocks, the immediate lesson is that these names now trade partly as AI proxies. That means Nvidia-specific news, even news about a boardroom reshuffle, can move them in ways that have little to do with Bitcoin itself. A few things are worth watching from here. The first is how Kress and the new board steady Nvidia, since GPU supply and pricing ripple straight through to the customers that miners host. The second is whether Texas lawmakers produce the electricity and water rules Hinojosa says are needed before the permit pause can lift. The third is financing. Miners that need to raise debt or equity in this environment may face steeper terms, which could squeeze the margins that made the AI pivot attractive in the first place.
